meta.title: CS50 Problems
meta.caveat: This is this repo's own _cs50psets pathway (a mix of CS50 AP-adapted and originally written problem sets), not Harvard's CS50 AP curriculum itself -- that's the separate cs50ap/cs50ap-extended carriers. Locators are this pathway's own order numbers (1-11), not CS50's own pset numbering. locator_slugs is still needed even though every page uses the collection's plain /cs50-psets/:name/ permalink, since a pset's filename slug (e.g. 'mario-less') isn't a predictable function of its locator number the way a zero-padded chapter number would be.

alignment_log.scope: First pass, all 6 pset pages (mario-less, pathfinder, palindromes, square, caesar, readability) against all four frameworks
alignment_log.note: Transcribed from a prior hand-authored 'Standards Alignment' section already present on each page (2026-08-26 formula, done pset-by-pset against the working-in-python source repo's catalog files before this repo had its own carrier system). Every cited code re-confirmed against this repo's own _standards/*.json catalog copies. A code a page had flagged 'headers only' (present but not the point of the problem) is carried here as strength: related rather than strong.

alignment_log.scope: Second pass, extending coverage to the four psets added since the first pass (Battery Gauge, Lineup less/more comfortable, Inheritance) against all four frameworks
alignment_log.note: Battery Gauge has no citable apcsp or csta2026 code: AP CSP's pseudocode has no try/except construct, and the closest csta2026 hits are cybersecurity-hygiene standards (input validation as one item in a script-safety or defense-in-depth list) too far from Battery's actual point to cite honestly. Its only new citation is an extension to the existing C4.9 entry. Lineup (less comfortable) similarly has thin coverage outside apcsp 3.10 (partial) and ca-ict-anchor C4.10 (not cited, see that entry's note) -- no catalog here names the queue/FIFO abstraction directly, only generic list operations or (in csta2026's S1-SWD-DD-01) library-provided structures its own scope note excludes hand-implemented internals from. Lineup (more comfortable) and Inheritance both had strong, direct hits across three of the four frameworks.

alignment_log.scope: New ngss catalog, applied to the two Profiling Float problems only (locators 13 and 14, added to this carrier in this pass); nothing else in this carrier was re-checked against NGSS
alignment_log.note: Read both problems' full text, including the Argo background, the specification parts and Going Further. Only the Engineering Design and two ocean-and-climate expectations are indexed. The two float problems are not yet carried against apcsp, castandards, csta2026 or ca-ict-anchor. Their front matter said chapter: 8, the Battery Gauge locator, so their pages had been showing Battery Gauge's standards; changed to 13 and 14 in this pass.

alignment_log.scope: The two Profiling Float problems (locators 13 and 14) against apcsp, castandards, csta2026 and ca-ict-anchor, in the same pass as their NGSS entries
alignment_log.note: Read both problems' starter code and specification. Where a code was already carried by an earlier pset, this pass added the locator and one sentence to the note, so a code keeps the strength it already had; entries were extended only where the float problem is at least that strong. Not carried on purpose: AP CSP 3.1 and 3.9, AP CSP 3.15 and CSTA HS-ALG-PS-04 (the noise in the simulators is random, but the student never uses randomness), and California 9-12.DA.11 (a model checked against real observations: the floats are never compared with a real pool).

alignment_log.scope: New ca-epc catalog (California Environmental Principles and Concepts), applied to Profiling Float (locator 13) only
alignment_log.note: Why this framework: SLVUSD's 2026-27 LCAP Goal 3 is Environmental Literacy, grounded in the CDE Blueprint for Environmental Literacy, and its metric 3.2 counts the grade levels and courses with at least one thematic unit tied to the EP&Cs. Only the Argo background touches it, so both codes are related. Profiling Float: PID has nothing for the EP&Cs. Nothing in the ROV cards was looked at.

alignment_log.scope: Profiling Float and Profiling Float: PID (locators 13 and 14) against the new mate-rov catalog, entered by hand
alignment_log.note: These four are direct links I checked against what each problem asks the student to write, not links inferred through shared standards. Not claimed: FLOAT.1 (no buoyancy engine is built), FLOAT.6 (no float design document), and anything in SAFE, ELEC or COMM.

2.1.note: Pathfinder: converting a two-digit hex byte into the character it represents, and back, is binary place-value one layer up -- hex digits are a compact stand-in for four bits at a time.

3.3.note: Readability: turning the Coleman-Liau formula into code is this in its most direct form. Profiling Float: PID: the controller is the formula kp * error + ki * total + kd * slope, with the slope worked out as a change divided by the seconds that passed.

3.4.note: Caesar and Readability walk a string one character at a time (rotating letters through ord()/chr(), or building up letter/word/sentence counts); Palindromes cleans a word down to its letters and compares it to its own reverse. All three treat a string as a sequence to be walked, not an opaque value.

3.5.note: Palindromes tests a word against its own reverse in one Boolean expression; Square tests whether a cell sits on the border the same way -- a Boolean expression doing work a nested conditional would do more verbosely. Profiling Float: in_band is one comparison chain that returns True or False, and held and touched_bottom decide on it.

3.6.note: Mario (less comfortable): the re-prompt loop until a valid height is entered. Profiling Float: decide picks SINK, RISE or IDLE with a three-way conditional. Profiling Float: PID: update clamps its output with conditionals, and the windup fix is a condition on the signs of the error and the output.

3.7.note: Square: the border-cell test reads like a nested condition even though it's written as a single Boolean expression -- present in spirit, not in the code's actual structure.

3.8.note: Mario's pyramid, Square's grid, Caesar's letter shift, and Readability's character scan are all iteration doing the actual work of the problem, not incidental to it. Profiling Float: touched_bottom and held walk the whole log, and held keeps a running count that restarts when a packet falls outside the band.

3.9.note: Mario (less comfortable): building the pyramid row by row is a small case of start-rough-then-refine. Palindromes: same, in miniature. Neither problem's real point is algorithm development -- it's a side effect of how the solution reads.

3.13.note: Pathfinder's optional helper function ('To Get Full Credit') is the thinnest instance -- headers only there. Square and Readability require a real helper function per sub-task; Caesar's shift-as-argument is the same decomposition idea applied to a command-line parameter. Profiling Float: four short functions with parameters and docstrings, each doctested. Profiling Float: PID: the student fills in one method of a class from its docstring.

5.6.note: Caesar: the cipher is a case study for why a tiny keyspace makes an encryption scheme breakable, even though the exam itself doesn't test encryption mechanics.

3.10.note: Lineup (less comfortable): enqueue/dequeue are built directly from the core list operations this standard names (append at the end, remove at a given index), applied with a specific FIFO discipline. The standard itself is about list operations in general, not the queue abstraction, so this is real but partial overlap. Profiling Float: the log is a list of two-number packets read by index, and the judging functions step through it. Plain list reading, not list operations, so the strength stays partial.

3.15.note: Inheritance: every allele, at every generation, comes from random.choice() rather than being computed -- the program's entire output varies run to run by design.

3.16.note: Inheritance builds a simulated family tree standing in for a real genetic process, trading biological realism (three alleles, uniform random inheritance, no linkage or dominance) for a repeatable, codeable model -- and EK AAP-3.F.8 (a simulation using a random number generator to mimic real-world unpredictability) is exactly create_family's mechanism. Profiling Float: the student works with three simulated floats, one fine and two flawed, and reads what each does. Profiling Float: PID: the simulator adds a constant bias, sensor noise and a slow motor, and the student tunes a controller by running it. In both the student uses a simulation as a stand-in for a pool and the pages say what it leaves out; the student does not write the simulator.

3.17.note: Lineup (more comfortable)'s whole point is this standard almost exactly: list.pop(0) and deque.popleft() solve the same problem at different speeds as the queue grows, discussed entirely in plain-language terms (shifting elements vs. not), matching this topic's own exclusion of formal Big-O analysis.

1.4.note: Profiling Float: PID: the windup bug is found by testing (the float is thrown through the hold depth), explained, and fixed. The student then comments the fix out to see the failure come back and writes down what happens.

2.3.note: Profiling Float: held reads a log of depth readings and gets a yes or no out of it, and the Argo explorer has the student compare temperature against depth for real floats in different oceans, including data that is not smooth.

9-12.AP.14.note: Mario, Palindromes, Square, and Readability all turn on a deliberate control-structure choice (loop vs. conditional vs. helper function) made concrete in each solution. Profiling Float: decide is a conditional, held is a loop with a counter, and the student has to pick which to use for each part.

9-12.AP.16.note: Square and Readability both require breaking the problem into named, reusable functions rather than one long script. Profiling Float: the judge is split into four named functions that each answer one question. Profiling Float: PID: the controller is one class with one method to complete. In both the split is given, and the student writes the pieces.

9-12.DA.8.note: Pathfinder and Caesar both convert between a character and a numeric representation of it -- the same letter can be written as a symbol or as a number, and moving between the two is the whole point of each problem.

9-12.NI.6.note: Caesar's own cipher, and why a small keyspace makes it breakable, is a direct case study for this standard.

9-12S.AP.13.note: Lineup (more comfortable)'s NOTE aside on deque vs. list is a plain-language version of exactly this: the same task (removing from the front) runs at very different speeds depending on the structure, without ever naming Big-O formally. This is the CA 9-12 Specialty (non-core) tier, one step beyond the core standards the earlier six psets cite.

9-12S.AP.14.note: Lineup (more comfortable) makes the data-structure choice explicit and consequential: deque over list for the queue (fast at both ends), plain list over deque for the history stack (fast at one end already, so the extra machinery buys nothing). Same CA 9-12 Specialty (non-core) tier as 9-12S.AP.13.

9-12S.AP.15.note: Inheritance's create_family is exactly this: a base case (generations == 1, no parents) and a recursive case (build both parents first, then choose alleles from them), and the Hints section explicitly walks through why the parents have to be built before this person's alleles can be chosen. Same CA 9-12 Specialty (non-core) tier as the two entries above.

9-12.AP.13.note: Profiling Float: a log is a list of packets, each a list of two numbers, in place of a pile of separate variables.

9-12.AP.20.note: Profiling Float: PID: tune, run the nine-pool check, read the result, change a gain and run it again; then find and fix the windup bug. The aim goes past working to holding the depth in every pool.

HS-ALG-PS-02.note: Every pset in this pathway is, at bottom, an algorithmic problem broken into steps and translated into code -- this is the one standard all ten currently share. Both Profiling Float problems turn a plain-language rule (hold 30 seconds in a row; keep the output within a limit) into steps.

HS-DAT-DC-24.note: Mario (less comfortable): the re-prompt loop is range-checking in practice -- is the value the right type, does it fall in a sensible range.

HS-PRO-PD-12.note: Square and Readability both require decomposing the problem into a helper function per sub-task rather than inlining everything. Profiling Float: a function per question the judge asks. Profiling Float: PID: a PID object that remembers its own gains, running total and last error.

HS-SYS-SE-33.note: Caesar's cipher is a case study in a system (the encryption scheme) whose security depends on its keyspace.

S1-SWD-DD-01.note: Lineup (more comfortable) names both structures this standard uses as its own examples: a queue (the song lineup, now on deque) and a stack (the history, on a plain list). Its scope note expects library-provided structures and their methods, not hand-implemented internals, which is why this is cited for the more-comfortable version (built on deque and list's own append/pop) and not the less-comfortable one, which implements the FIFO discipline itself on a bare list.

HS-ALG-PS-03.note: Lineup (more comfortable) compares list.pop(0) and deque.popleft() informally, by reasoning about what each has to do, not a formal proof -- exactly the comparison basis this standard's scope note allows.

HS-ALG-PS-04.note: Inheritance's Usage section says outright that a student's own output won't match the example run, since alleles are chosen randomly every time -- the exact distinction this standard names, explained in plain terms with no probability calculation required.

HS-PRO-TR-20.note: Profiling Float: PID: the check results change the program: the gains move after each run, and the windup bug found by the test is fixed in update.

HS-DAT-DI-26.note: Profiling Float: the explorer says the data is not the final cleaned-up version and why the curves wiggle. Profiling Float: PID: Going Further asks whether the best tuning in a simulated pool is one to trust in a real one. Neither asks the student to find a chart that misleads, so this is adjacent.

HS-PRO-RD-17.note: Profiling Float: PID: the student is told to read the given simulator, where each of the three real-world problems is one line, before tuning against it.

C2.2.note: Caesar: headers only -- the cipher touches basic security concepts without the problem asking students to reason about them directly.

C4.4.note: Pathfinder and Caesar both convert data between representations (hex byte to character, letter to shift number) -- data has types, and those types get encoded in specific ways.

C4.9.note: Mario, Palindromes, Square, Caesar, and Readability all lean on the same programming toolkit (loops, conditionals, functions with parameters) this standard names. Battery Gauge adds the toolkit's "ways to recover from errors" clause (its try/except retry loop), not demonstrated by any of the first six psets; Inheritance adds "a function that calls itself" (create_family and print_family are both recursive). Profiling Float: conditionals, a loop with a counter, and functions with parameters. Profiling Float: PID: a class with state (total, last) that a method reads and updates on every call.

C5.4.note: Square: running check50 against a solution makes testing a distinct, visible step rather than an afterthought. Both Profiling Float problems have the student run doctests and add at least one example of their own, so testing is a separate step. Profiling Float: PID: the nine-pool check is a second, bigger test.

C4.10.note: Lineup (more comfortable)'s central point is exactly this trade-off: a queue built on deque instead of a plain list. Lineup (less comfortable) introduces the queue itself but doesn't compare it against an alternative implementation, so it isn't cited here.

C5.6.note: Profiling Float: PID: the windup bug is a debugging task in the middle of a tuning task: reproduce it, understand it, fix it, and confirm the fix.

C4.8.note: Profiling Float: PID: a PID class with properties (kp, ki, kd, limit, total, last) and a method, which the starter code explains (class, self). The student completes one method and does not design a class or use inheritance, so this is partial.

MS-ETS1-1.note: Profiling Float: the criteria come from the competition task (stay within 0.33 m of the hold depth for 30 seconds in a row, do not touch the bottom), so the student does not define them. The student does turn them into precise, testable rules, in_band and held, which is the testable-criteria half of this expectation.

MS-ETS1-3.note: Profiling Float: the student reads the data packets of three simulated floats, one fine and two flawed, and decides which meets the criteria and why the others fail. That is the analyze-test-data half of this expectation. The combine-the-best-features half is only touched by the Going Further 'Fix the floats' item.

MS-ETS1-4.note: Both problems run a student's program against a simulated pool and use the results to improve it. Profiling Float: the simulator is given, and the iteration is light (steer, check the three floats). Profiling Float: PID: the iteration is the point (tune kp, ki, kd and write down what each change did; fix the windup bug found by testing), which would be strong on its own. The student uses a model here but does not build one.

HS-ETS1-4.note: A computer simulation of a float in a pool is the test bench for both problems. Profiling Float: PID is closest: its simulator adds a constant bias, sensor noise and a slow motor, and a controller passes only if it holds in all nine pools, so it is tested across a range of conditions. The simulator is given, not built, and it models one float, not a system with many interacting criteria.

HS-ETS1-3.note: Both judge a design against stated pass criteria (hold 30 seconds, stay off the bottom, score +5 and -5), and Going Further asks whether the best tuning is one to trust in a real pool. The criteria are not prioritized against each other and no cost, safety or environmental trade-off is asked for, so this is adjacent only.

HS-ETS1-2.note: Profiling Float is split for the student into four small functions (steer, touched the bottom, in the band, held) that together judge a float. The splitting is given, not something the student works out.

MS-ESS2-6.note: Profiling Float's Argo background and explorer let students compare temperature against depth for floats in different oceans. No model of circulation or regional climate is asked for; this is context only.

HS-ESS2-4.note: The background says the ocean takes up most of the extra heat from global warming and that floats are how it is watched. Context only: nothing asks the student to model energy flow or climate.

III.C.note: Profiling Float: the Argo background says the ocean takes up most of the extra heat from global warming and about a quarter of the carbon dioxide people release, and that floats are how scientists watch it happen. It is a background paragraph and the explorer graphs real profiles; no question asks the student to explain how a human practice changes a natural cycle.

IV.B.note: Profiling Float: the same paragraph is an example of a by-product (carbon dioxide, heat) entering a natural system, and the explorer shows what the floats measure. Context only, so adjacent, not taught.

FLOAT.2.note: Profiling Float: PID has the student build the controller that holds the top of a float at 2.0 meters, within 0.33 meters, for 30 seconds in a row, tested in nine simulated pools with a bias, noise and a slow motor. Profiling Float has the student judge whether a float held. Partial because it is a simulated float: no buoyancy hardware, no real sensor, and no allowing for a sensor that is not at the top of the float (only a Going Further item in Profiling Float).

FLOAT.3.note: Profiling Float: the student reads and judges a log of packets, but each packet has only a time and a depth. The company number, temperature, light and units of the real defined packet are not part of what the student writes, and nothing is transmitted.

FLOAT.4.note: Profiling Float: reading the packets for the five depths on the way up is the extra credit item (rungs), not the main problem.

FLOAT.5.note: Profiling Float: the student reads real temperature against depth graphs from Argo floats in the explorer but does not make a graph.
